props.title: Body Bags
props.initialSlug: Three twisted tales of terror and suspense

sections.content: John Carpenter's Body Bags represents a fascinating entry in the horror anthology format, following in the footsteps of Creepshow (1982) and Tales from the Darkside: The Movie (1990). Carpenter himself appears as a ghoulish mortician-host, clearly paying homage to Rod Serling's The Twilight Zone (1959-1964) while adding his own macabre spin. The film's three segments - "The Gas Station," "Hair," and "Eye" - showcase different horror styles, from slasher to body horror to psychological thriller, with Carpenter directing two segments and Tobe Hooper helming the third.

sections.content: The first segment, "The Gas Station," epitomizes the slasher subgenre that Carpenter helped popularize with Halloween (1978). It follows a female gas station attendant during her first night shift, creating claustrophobic tension reminiscent of Carpenter's siege film Assault on Precinct 13 (1976). The second story, "Hair," features Stacy Keach in a darkly comic body horror tale that shares DNA with The Thing (1982), while the final segment, "Eye," stars Mark Hamill in a psychological descent that echoes elements of Angel Heart (1987).

The film's impressive roster of horror veterans includes not just Carpenter and Hooper, but also special effects maestro Rick Baker, whose work here recalls his groundbreaking transformations in An American Werewolf in London (1981). The anthology format allows for experimentation with different horror styles, from the practical effects-driven body horror to more subtle psychological terror. sections.content: Body Bags arrived during a renaissance of horror anthologies in the early 1990s, following successful series like Tales from the Crypt (1989-1996) and preceding films like Tales from the Hood (1995). Its influence can be seen in later anthology projects like Trick 'r Treat (2007) and V/H/S (2012), which similarly use wraparound segments to connect their stories. The film's blend of established horror directors and genre stars would become a template for projects like Masters of Horror (2005-2007).
